items.before: The following passage is an extract from the letter. Read it carefully and answer the questions that follow.
items.after: The passage above is an extract from the letter. Read it carefully and answer the questions that follow.

periods.activity_title: Reading and Activating Prior Thought on Dreams

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reflect and Respond (p.231): four oral warm-up prompts on dreams and inspiration
Reading for Meaning (p.231): web chart — reasons why following a dream matters

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the letter format and its author, Irene Chua, with a brief orienting note about the collection. Students are invited to share what they understand by the phrase 'follow that dream' before reading begins.

The letter is read aloud by the teacher with students following in their textbooks (p.231–237), observing how the mother moves from encouragement to caution and back. Students note the conversational, direct-address tone as they listen.

Reflect and Respond (p.231): teacher facilitates a brief paired exchange on the four oral prompts — students share what their dream is, who inspires them, what qualities are needed, and discuss the Abdul Kalam quotation as a class.

Reading for Meaning web chart (p.231): students individually fill in as many reasons as they can for why following a dream is important, then two or three volunteers share entries aloud for a quick whole-class check.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens with the full text read-aloud so that every student has a shared encounter with the letter before discussion begins. The letter's episodic structure — personal anecdote, rhetorical questions, and measured caution — is worth pointing out so students do not expect a straightforward argument essay. An uncovered task (the role of parents and community, task index 1) may be suggested as a reflective note students jot informally.
materials: Blackboard or chart paper for web chart entries

periods.activity_title: True/False Comprehension Check and Extract Close-Reading

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Check Your Understanding (p.234): seven true/false statements on the letter's key arguments
Critical Reflection Extract 1 (p.235–236): five analytical sub-questions on passion, conviction, and stamina

time_bands.activity: Teacher directs students back to the letter to verify each of the seven true/false statements (p.234) by locating supporting evidence in the text. Students work in pairs, then answers are confirmed whole-class with textual justification.

Students re-read the Extract 1 passage (p.235) closely and individually draft responses to the first two sub-questions — the analogy fill-in and the MCQ on why a realistic assessment of effort matters. Teacher circulates and prompts evidence-based reasoning.

The remaining three sub-questions of Extract 1 (the word 'plunge,' intrinsic motivation, and a motivating factor beyond success) are handled through open whole-class discussion, with the teacher modelling how to embed textual phrases into a short constructed response.

Teacher consolidates by asking students to articulate in one sentence the mother's core argument about effort and sacrifice, drawing on evidence from Extract 1. Two or three responses are shared aloud to close the unit.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the full letter aloud in the previous sitting, students now move from initial impression to closer scrutiny of the argument. A common pitfall is treating the true/false statements as memory recall rather than evidence-finding; push students to cite the exact lines that support or contradict each statement. The ECR-type questions (how Ming's mother balances encouragement with caution, task index 6 items d–e) are left unanchored here; they will be addressed in the next reading unit.

periods.activity_title: Analytical Deep Dive — Extract 2 and Extended Response

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Critical Reflection Extract 2 (p.236): five sub-questions on evolving dreams and the mother's tone
Answer the Following (p.236–237): three SCR and three ECR questions on persuasion, balance, and contemporary relevance

time_bands.activity: Students work individually on Extract 2 (p.236), answering all five sub-questions — fill-in, two SCRs, an extract-phrase identification, and the tone MCQ. Teacher pauses the class at the midpoint to discuss the concept of 'evolving dreams' before students complete their written responses.

From the Answer the Following set (p.236–237), teacher leads a whole-class discussion of the first three questions — what Ming may have written, how to attain international skill, and what differentiates dreamers from achievers. Students are expected to phrase answers in complete sentences with textual grounding.

Students write an individual extended response to one of the two ECR prompts — either how the mother uses anecdote and rhetoric to persuade, or how she balances encouragement with caution. Responses are written in the exercise book; the teacher circulates and offers brief formative comments on structure and textual evidence use.

periods.teacher_notes: Having worked through Extract 1's argument about effort and sacrifice, students are now ready to engage with the letter's reflective, personal dimension — the mother's own evolving dream of publishing a book. A common pitfall is conflating 'optimistic and encouraging' with 'appreciative and celebratory' in the tone question; direct students to the explicit word choices in the extract. The contemporary relevance ECR (task index 6, item f) and the oral costs-and-sacrifice prompt (task index 6, item g) are left unanchored; flag these to students as strong independent reflection prompts.

periods.activity_title: Listening to an Announcement, Then Role-Play on Pursuing a Dream

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Listen and Respond (p.241): fill in six blanks with exact words from the vocational-courses announcement
Speaking Activity (p.241–242): four-role group role-play on pursuing a dream as trekking guide

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefs students on attentive listening — they should hold pencils ready but not write until they hear the key information. The purpose and format of the announcement (vocational courses) is described in a single sentence so students know what to listen for.

Teacher reads or plays the school announcement (transcript p.275) twice. Students fill in the six blanks on p.241 with exact words; teacher then verifies answers whole-class, asking students to identify the phrases that gave them each answer.

Teacher introduces the role-play scenario (p.241–242) — a student dreaming of becoming a trekking guide — and assigns the four roles within groups of four. Groups briefly plan their responses using the sentence prompts given for each role.

Groups perform their role-plays; two or three groups share with the class. Teacher uses a brief whole-class debrief to draw out how each role's language differed in register and purpose, connecting back to the letter's theme of balancing passion with realism.

periods.teacher_notes: Having engaged deeply with the mother's written argument about dreams, students now encounter the same theme through two oral modes — receptive (listening) and productive (speaking). The announcement's fill-in task requires attention to exact phrasing, so caution students against paraphrasing. In the role-play, watch that the Parent and Mentor roles do not collapse into the same position; the sentence prompts in the textbook deliberately differentiate them — point this out during the planning phase.
materials: Transcript (p.275 of transcript booklet) or audio playback device

periods.activity_title: Drafting a Formal Email to a Design Institute

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Writing Task (p.242): formal email to a design institute enquiring about a summer workshop

time_bands.activity: Teacher models the structural components of a formal email on the board — header (sender, receiver, date, subject), introduction, body with specific enquiries, conclusion, and complementary close — using a neutral example. Students identify each component and note what formal register demands: no abbreviations, complete sentences, appropriate salutation.

Students plan their email in rough — listing the four or five pieces of information they need to ask about (fees, duration, eligibility, schedule, outcomes) and drafting a one-sentence introduction that states who they are and why they are writing. Teacher circulates and checks that each student has a clear purpose statement before proceeding.

Students write the full email draft in their exercise books, following the guidelines on p.242. Teacher circulates, offering brief formative comments on register (flagging any informal phrasing), completeness of the header, and whether the body paragraphs follow the introduction–enquiry–conclusion structure.

Students exchange drafts with a partner for a quick peer review focused on two criteria only: formal language maintained throughout, and all required header fields present. Two volunteers read their emails aloud; class offers one specific improvement suggestion each.

periods.teacher_notes: The writing task connects naturally to the letter's theme — the mother's discussion of passion translated into action — since students are now writing as a person taking a concrete step toward a dream. A common pitfall is students slipping into informal register in the body paragraphs after a correctly formal opening; the peer-review step is designed to catch exactly this. The entire drafting and peer-response cycle is completed within this unit so no written artefact from another sitting is required.

periods.activity_title: Vocabulary in Context — '-scape' Words, Idioms, and Modal 'Could'

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.237): '-scape' compound words — dictionary lookup and dialogue fill-in
Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.238–239): six idiomatic expressions — choose meaning and use in a sentence
Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.239): modal 'could' — match four sentences to their functions

homework.task_brief: Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.239): first conditional — complete five sentences using imperatives

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the '-scape' suffix using the word 'dreamscape' from the letter (p.237). Students use dictionaries to find meanings of mindscape, seascape, landscape, and cityscape, then complete the four-blank dialogue with the correct '-scape' word; answers are verified whole-class.

Idiom task (p.238–239): students work through all six multiple-choice questions independently, choosing the best meaning for each underlined expression. For the first three idioms, students additionally write one original sentence using the expression; teacher checks that the sentence context matches the idiom's meaning, not just its surface words.

Modal 'could' matching task (p.239): teacher briefly explains the four functions of 'could' (possibility, unreal/hypothetical, past possibility/speculation, past ability/purpose) using one example each on the board. Students then match the four textbook sentences to their functions and share answers, with teacher reinforcing the reasoning for each.

Quick consolidation: teacher writes two fresh sentences on the board using 'could' and asks students to identify the function. Sets homework — the first conditional task (p.239) — explaining that completing sentences with appropriate imperatives reinforces the conditional structure met in the letter.

periods.teacher_notes: The vocabulary cluster in this unit is drawn directly from the letter's language — 'dreamscape,' 'coursing through her veins,' 'wet blanket,' 'uphill' — so students encounter grammar in its living context rather than in isolation. The 'could' task is the conceptually denser element; a common pitfall is conflating 'past possibility/speculation' with 'past ability' — the board examples should make the temporal and modal distinctions explicit. Tasks on filling in grammatical forms in a passage (task index 5) are left unanchored; flag them as a self-study grammar consolidation exercise.

periods.activity_title: Vision Board and Local Inspiration Research Presentation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Learning Beyond the Text (p.243–244): create a personal Vision Board across five sections
Learning Beyond the Text (p.244–257): research a local inspiring personality and present their story

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the Vision Board concept (p.243) by walking through the five sections: My Dreams, I Want to Try, Goals, Places I Will Go, and Inspiration. Students are given A4 paper and told they will work through the five sections in a condensed written-and-drawn form.

Students create their Vision Boards individually — writing or sketching content for each of the five sections on p.243–244. Teacher circulates, encouraging specificity (a named goal rather than 'success') and prompting quiet students with the examples of Shivaji, Madalasa, and Kalam that the textbook provides.

Teacher introduces the local-personality research task (p.244–257) using the three textbook examples — Chhatrapati Shivaji, Queen Madalasa, and Dr. APJ Abdul Kalam — as models for the structure of a success story: challenge faced, parental or community support, and outcome. Students briefly note (in a few bullet points) a personality they know from their own village, town, or state.

Four to five volunteers share their chosen personality and what they have noted, presenting informally to the class. Teacher facilitates brief discussion after each, connecting the presented story back to the letter's argument that community and support networks are essential to realising a dream.

periods.teacher_notes: The Vision Board and the local-personality research are complementary — one is inward-facing (personal aspiration) and one is outward-facing (community evidence of dreams realised). Both are completed within this unit. Students who have not identified a local personality in time for the sharing phase can draw on the textbook examples; there is no dependency on prior research work outside class.
materials: A4 paper and coloured pens or pencils for Vision Boards

items.source_lo: Student analyses authorial purpose, tone, and persuasive structure using informational prose as the vehicle.
items.source_context: A mother's letter urging Ming to weigh sacrifice, conviction, and community before committing to a dream.
items.item_stem:
Read the statements below and write True or False for each. If false, write a corrected version in one sentence.
(1) The mother in the letter argues that world-class mastery in any field can be achieved in a few months of focused practice.
(2) The mother uses the example of Academy Award winners to show that individual achievement always depends on a support community.
(3) The mother believes that circumstances such as war and poverty have no bearing on whether a person can realise their dream.

options.text: The mother believes that circumstances such as war and poverty have no bearing on whether a person can realise their dream.
The mother in the letter argues that world-class mastery in any field can be achieved in a few months of focused practice.
The mother uses the example of Academy Award winners to show that individual achievement always depends on a support community.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: (1) False — the mother states that world-class mastery typically demands at least ten years of singular, intensive pursuit. (2) True — she invokes Academy Award winners who always thank a support network as evidence that even individual achievement rests on community. (3) False — the mother explicitly references people whose dreams were derailed by the Japanese invasion of World War II and by family financial obligations.

items.source_lo: Student analyses authorial purpose, tone, and persuasive structure using informational prose as the vehicle.
items.source_context: A mother's letter urging Ming to weigh sacrifice, conviction, and community before committing to a dream.
items.item_stem:
The passage above is an extract from the letter. Read it carefully and answer the questions that follow.

1. The mother says the uphill road is sustained only by knowing one is doing what one loves and doing the right thing. What does this reveal about how she views the relationship between intrinsic motivation and perseverance?
2. The mother shifts from encouraging Ming to introducing examples of people whose dreams were destroyed by the Japanese invasion and family poverty. Analyse how this shift serves her persuasive purpose in the letter.
3. The letter closes with the mother reflecting on how her own dream of publishing a book evolved over a decade. What does this personal disclosure add to her authority as an adviser, and what does it reveal about her attitude toward dreams changing over time?
items.visual_stimulus: The mother argues that the uphill road is sustained only by the knowledge that one is doing what one loves and doing the right thing; when stamina falters, the prospect of success provides the necessary momentum. She then cautions that many people never move beyond wishful thinking, and that circumstances — war, poverty, family obligation — have derailed the dreams of entire generations. She references people whose aspirations to attend Raffles College were destroyed by the Japanese invasion of World War II, and others who sacrificed their own schooling to support siblings financially. She closes by reflecting on how her own dream of publishing a book evolved over a decade from her youthful ambitions, and expresses the hope that at least one of Ming's dreams will come true.

expected_elements: Links intrinsic motivation to sustained effort when external rewards are absent.
Identifies the shift as a rhetorical move — grounding caution in historical, not personal, risk.
Recognises that real obstacles (war, poverty) make the caution credible rather than discouraging.
Acknowledges the personal disclosure builds ethos — mother as co-dreamer, not just adviser.
Notes that evolving dreams are framed as growth, not failure, aligning with the letter's hopeful tone.

items.source_lo: Student extracts specific details and key information accurately from a listened announcement using informational listening as the vehicle.
items.source_context: A school announcement about new vocational courses — eligibility, registration dates, and seat limits.
items.item_stem:
Listen to the school announcement about the new vocational courses. As you listen, decide whether each statement below is True or False.
(1) Any student in the school, regardless of grade, may register for a vocational course.
(2) Each student who registers may choose a maximum of one course.
(3) Registration forms will be available from the school office starting on a Monday.

options.text: Any student in the school, regardless of grade, may register for a vocational course.
Each student who registers may choose a maximum of one course.
Registration forms will be available from the school office starting on a Monday.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: (1) False — the announcement states that only students from Grades 9 to 12 are eligible. (2) True — each student can choose only one course. (3) True — forms are available from the school office starting Monday, 04 April.

items.source_lo: Student extracts specific details and key information accurately from a listened announcement using informational listening as the vehicle.
items.source_context: A school announcement about new vocational courses — eligibility, registration dates, and seat limits.
items.item_stem:
After listening to the announcement, answer the following questions in one or two sentences each.
(a) Why might a student who submits her form on Friday, 08 April, still not receive her first choice of course?
(b) The announcement states that courses are conducted by trained professionals at the school. Why is this detail significant for students deciding whether to register?

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: (a) Seats are limited and preference is given to early applicants, so a student submitting on the final day may find her preferred course already full. (b) Knowing that trained professionals — not regular teachers — will conduct the courses signals a higher level of specialised instruction, making the courses more credible for real-world skill development.

items.source_lo: Student argues, negotiates, and supports a position using assigned perspective and role-specific language in a structured role-play.
items.source_context: Four-role scenario — dreamer, parent, mentor, friend — debating whether to pursue trekking guiding as a career.
items.item_stem: You are assigned the role of the Dreamer in a group discussion. Your classmate wants to give up her plan to become a wildlife photographer because her family is worried about financial security. Recount your own dream and describe two specific steps you have taken — or plan to take — to show that it is achievable, using evidence or examples to reassure your classmate.

expected_elements: Clearly names the speaker's own dream with a reason for choosing it.
Describes at least two concrete, realistic steps toward achieving the dream.
Uses reassuring, direct-address language appropriate to a peer conversation.
Cites at least one real-world example or evidence of the dream being viable.
Maintains the Dreamer's perspective throughout without slipping into the Mentor's register.

items.source_lo: Student argues, negotiates, and supports a position using assigned perspective and role-specific language in a structured role-play.
items.source_context: Four-role scenario — dreamer, parent, mentor, friend — debating whether to pursue trekking guiding as a career.
items.item_stem: Your class is holding an open-house dialogue on the proposition: 'Financial security should always come before following an unconventional dream.' Take a clear position — for or against — and argue your case with at least two reasons, one of which must draw on a real or plausible example of someone who did or did not prioritise security over their passion.

expected_elements: States a clear position at the outset and maintains it throughout.
Offers at least two distinct reasons supporting the stated position.
Incorporates a real or plausible example relevant to the argument.
Anticipates and briefly addresses one counterargument.
Uses persuasive, well-organised language with appropriate formal register for a dialogue.

items.item_stem: Your school has announced that it will send a team to an inter-school science fair organised by a regional university next term. You are keen to participate. Write a formal email to the Event Coordinator of the university requesting details about registration, team size, eligible topics, and the submission deadline. Follow the standard email format: header (sender, receiver, date, subject), introduction, body with specific enquiries, conclusion, and complementary close.

expected_elements: Complete header: sender, receiver, date, and a precise subject line.
Formal register maintained throughout — no abbreviations or contractions.
Introduction identifies the writer and clearly states the purpose.
Body raises at least three specific, relevant enquiries in separate sentences.
Closing and complementary close (e.g. 'Yours sincerely') correctly formatted.

items.item_stem: A local newspaper has published an editorial arguing that schools spend too much time on arts, sports, and 'impractical' subjects, and should focus exclusively on mathematics and science to prepare students for employment. Write a letter to the editor responding to this view. Argue your position clearly, support it with at least two reasons, and acknowledge one valid aspect of the editorial's concern before refuting its central claim. Use the correct letter-to-the-editor format.

expected_elements: Correct letter-to-editor format: date, editor's address, salutation, sign-off.
Clear position stated in the opening paragraph without ambiguity.
At least two well-developed reasons supporting the writer's argument.
Acknowledges one genuine concern raised by the editorial before countering it.
Persuasive, formal register sustained; no informal phrasing or unsupported generalisations.

items.source_lo: Student interprets idiomatic expressions and modal verbs in context and applies word-formation knowledge drawn from the text.
items.source_context: Idioms from the letter ('uphill,' 'wet blanket,' 'coursing through your veins') and modal 'could' in its varied functions.
items.item_stem:
Each sentence below uses the modal verb 'could'. For each sentence, (a) identify the function of 'could' from the options in brackets, and (b) write one new sentence of your own using 'could' in the same function.

(1) 'It could be in any field — sports, science, arts, business or design.' [Possibility / Past ability / Unreal situation]
(2) 'I wish I could pursue every dream without worrying about time.' [Possibility / Unreal or hypothetical / Past speculation]
(3) 'She could have chosen a safer path, but she didn't.' [Past possibility or speculation / Formal request / Present ability]

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: (1) Possibility — 'could' indicates that the field is not fixed; any of many fields is a genuine option. Example: 'The solution could be simpler than we think.' (2) Unreal or hypothetical — 'could' with 'wish' signals an imagined, non-real situation. Example: 'I wish I could travel the world for free.' (3) Past possibility or speculation — 'could have' indicates something was possible in the past but did not happen. Example: 'He could have taken the earlier bus, but he missed it.'

items.item_stem: Write a short paragraph (6–8 sentences) describing your Vision Board. In your paragraph, explain: (a) what your most important dream is and why you chose it, (b) one specific goal you have set to move toward that dream, and (c) who or what in your life inspires you most. Your paragraph should make the connection between your personal inspiration and the concrete steps on your Vision Board clear.

expected_elements: Names one significant personal dream with a reason for its importance.
States one concrete, realistic goal as a step toward that dream.
Identifies a specific source of personal inspiration (person, event, value).
Makes a clear logical connection between inspiration, goal, and dream.
Writes in coherent paragraphs with adequate sentence variety for Grade IX.

items.item_stem: Research a personality from your own village, town, city, or state who overcame significant challenges — social, financial, or circumstantial — to achieve a notable goal. Prepare a short presentation (spoken or written, as your teacher directs) covering: (a) the challenge(s) the person faced, (b) the community or family support that helped them, (c) the outcome of their efforts, and (d) one lesson from their story that you find personally relevant. Use at least one reliable source and name it in your presentation.

expected_elements: Names a real, identifiable local personality with a brief introduction.
Describes at least two specific challenges faced — not vague generalisations.
Identifies concrete community or family support that contributed to success.
States the outcome clearly and connects it to the effort described.
Draws a personally relevant lesson and cites at least one named source.
